strengths: The reported results are promising for ImageNet-scale dataset distillation. At 50 images per class, Table 1 reports 57.6% on ImageNet-1K versus CDA's 53.5%, and 59.4% on Tiny-ImageNet versus 48.7%. These would be practically meaningful improvements if established under matched protocols.
Combining pretrained feature targets with class-specific BatchNorm statistics provides a straightforward distillation pipeline that avoids differentiating through student training.

Evaluation covers three datasets, multiple compression budgets, three-run accuracy measurements, component ablations, hyperparameter sensitivity, and transfer to other architectures. Table 2 provides encouraging evidence of transfer within the ResNet family.

The manuscript attributes its datasets, optimal-transport machinery, and SRe2L foundation. The supplement supplies pseudocode and several training settings, and acknowledges source-data bias, computational overhead, and dependence on a pretrained classifier.
weaknesses: The central contribution is insufficiently distinguished from feature-space clustering. With squared Euclidean cost and freely optimized support weights, Eq. (7) reduces to ordinary k-means quantization: minimizing the average squared distance to the nearest prototype. This equivalence and a clustering-based baseline are missing. At one image per class, the target is simply the class feature mean, also targeted by linear-kernel MMD in the same feature space. Consequently, Table 4 does not isolate a metric advantage without matching the encoder and regularization; removing augmentation and FKD alone is insufficient.

The ablations provide limited evidence that Wasserstein matching drives the improvements. Holding cross-entropy and class-specific BatchNorm fixed, adding barycenter matching changes ImageNette accuracy from 64.0% to 63.9%, Tiny-ImageNet from 41.3% to 42.1%, and ImageNet from 37.4% to 37.9% (Table 3). These modest differences contrast with the paper's emphasis on the metric. Corresponding ablations at 50 and 100 images per class, where the strongest results occur, are needed.

The baseline discrepancy materially weakens the headline comparison. At 10 images per class on ImageNet, Table 1 reports 21.3% for SRe2L, whereas Table 3's described baseline achieves 36.1%. The manuscript does not adequately reconcile the protocols producing this difference. Against the latter baseline, the proposed method's 38.2% represents a substantially smaller improvement.

The optimized distribution is not clearly preserved by the final pipeline. Equations (6)-(15) learn nonuniform masses, but Algorithm 1 returns only images, Eq. (16) matches support locations without those masses, and weighted student sampling is not specified. Matching these locations with uniformly sampled images need not reproduce the Wasserstein-optimized distribution.

The optimization explanation needs correction. Section 4.2.2's convexity argument applies with the transport plan fixed, not globally after optimizing that plan. Algorithm 2 also updates weights without specifying a new coupling before the position update, and permits zero weights despite updates involving their reciprocals. These issues leave the claimed optimization behavior inadequately justified.

Efficiency and reproducibility evidence is incomplete. Table 6 measures only ImageNette at one image per class, where the barycenter reduces to a mean; it does not substantiate transport overhead at larger ImageNet budgets. The manuscript also leaves barycenter initialization, solver settings, and stopping criteria insufficiently specified. End-to-end timing should clarify the inclusion of teacher training, feature extraction, barycenter computation, and relabeling.
